passage: Vinita, in my day we had no hearts or thumbs, and somehow we worried just the same. When I was seventeen I once wrote a long letter to a friend, and she didn't reply for three weeks. I decided she didn't like me. Then I found out her family had moved cities. You have those little reaction buttons now, and I've seen you go quiet when a friend didn't tap one on your post. Remember my letter. A thumbs-up is a quick way to say 'I saw you, well done', and it costs nothing to give. But when it doesn't come, it usually means she was busy, or asleep, or the phone was off. Ask her at lunch. Rafiq, your grandfather.

qa.q: How long did the friend not reply to Rafiq's letter?
qa.a: She did not reply for three weeks.

qa.q: Why did Rafiq decide the friend didn't like him?
qa.a: He felt hurt by the silence and assumed the worst, before learning that her family had moved cities. His story shows how easily a missing signal is over-read.

qa.q: What advice does Rafiq give Vinita when a friend does not react to Vinita's post?
qa.a: Do not read it as rejection, and simply ask the friend in person.

qa.q: How might Vinita's friend feel if Vinita went quiet over a missing thumbs-up?
qa.a: She might be surprised and upset, since she may not even have noticed the post.

grounding: An elder says reaction buttons are lightweight signals, and a missing reaction should not be over-read.

passage: It was the night before exams, the power kept flickering, and Parul's phone had one bar of signal. She posted a photo of her notes with the caption 'wish me luck', then tapped a heart on Harish's post about his last revision session. Harish, at his desk with a candle beside him, saw her heart and felt lighter. She waited. Nobody reacted to hers for an hour. Her stomach dropped. Then she remembered what her grandfather had said and told herself: the network is bad and everybody is studying. She switched it off and went back to the chapter. In the morning, Harish sent, 'Good luck! I saw your post late, network was down.' She smiled and put her pen in her bag.

qa.q: What did Parul tap on Harish's post?
qa.a: She tapped a heart.

qa.q: Why did Parul's stomach drop when nobody reacted?
qa.a: She felt worried that people didn't care or that she was not supported, at a stressful time. Then she reminded herself that the network and studying could explain it.

qa.q: What did Parul do that helped her cope?
qa.a: She reminded herself of a likelier explanation and put the phone away to study.

qa.q: How might Harish have felt when he saw Parul's heart?
qa.a: He felt lighter, since the heart was a quick sign of support during a tense night.

grounding: Reaction buttons are lightweight signals, and a missing reaction should not be over-read.

passage:
Chandrika uploaded her first song cover on a Friday night: a slow old Hindi song, recorded on her phone in the bathroom for the echo. She sent the link to the class group.
Hearts came quickly. Thumbs-up. A few fire emojis. By midnight, thirty reactions.
But not from Ujjwal. Her best friend since Class 2.
She checked at one. At seven. At ten. Nothing. Was he embarrassed for her? Did he hate it?
By Saturday afternoon she'd convinced herself he thought it was terrible.
Then at four, a message: "CHANDRIKA. Just got network at Nani's village. Listened three times on the bus stand. The second verse!!! 🤍"
She laughed out loud in the kitchen. Her mother looked over.
"Nothing," Chandrika said, grinning. "Just a very late heart."
She wrote in her notes app: no reaction is not a reaction.

qa.q: How many reactions did the cover have by midnight?
qa.a: By midnight, thirty reactions.

qa.q: What was Chandrika feeling while waiting for Ujjwal's reaction?
qa.a: Chandrika felt anxious and hurt, reading the missing reaction as a sign he thought the song was terrible.

qa.q: What could Chandrika remember next time a reaction is missing?
qa.a: A missing reaction may simply mean no network or no time, so it shouldn't be read as rejection.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal have felt reading Chandrika's worry, if she told him?
qa.a: He would probably have felt surprised and sorry, since he loved the song and was only out of network.

grounding: The scene shows reactions as quick support signals and a missing reaction wrongly over-read as rejection.

passage:
"You just thumbs-upped it."
Sharmila looked up from her locker. "What?"
"My message. About getting into the state team. I wrote a whole paragraph, and you sent a thumbs-up."
Jomon's arms were folded.
"Oh! Jomon, I was in the middle of the maths test. I saw it under the desk and panicked and hit the first thing."
"It looked like you didn't care."
"I care so much! State team! That's huge!" She hugged her books. "I meant to write properly after and then forgot. That's on me."
Jomon's arms loosened. "Okay. I thought maybe you were jealous or something."
"Of your bowling? A bit, obviously." She grinned. "But mostly proud. Can I buy you a samosa?"
"Two samosas."
"Two samosas."
That evening she sent him a long voice note, and he replied with one thumbs-up, on purpose.

qa.q: What was Jomon's message about?
qa.a: About getting into the state team.

qa.q: What was Jomon feeling about the thumbs-up?
qa.a: Jomon felt hurt and a little suspicious, reading the tiny reaction as not caring or even jealousy.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what fixed it?
qa.a: A quick thumbs-up sent during a test looked like indifference; talking face to face and following up with a proper voice note fixed it.

qa.q: How might Sharmila have seen her thumbs-up at the time?
qa.a: She saw it as a quick, excited acknowledgement in a hurry, not realising how small it would look next to his big news.

grounding: The dialogue shows a thumbs-up as a lightweight signal being over-read as rejection, and a clear follow-up repairing it.

passage:
Last year, when my friend Eshaan's grandfather was in hospital, he stopped talking much at school. He'd post one line on his status some nights: "long day." "tired."
I didn't know what to say. So I just reacted with a heart every time. Sometimes a folded-hands one. I worried that it was too small, that he'd think I was lazy.
Months later he told me the hearts helped. "I didn't want to talk. But I'd see yours and know someone saw it."
It went the other way too. After his grandfather got better, Eshaan stopped reacting to my posts for weeks. I started wondering if I'd done something wrong. Then I remembered the hearts. Sometimes you're just busy living.
I asked him once, lightly. He said, "Sorry, I've just been off my phone."
Small signals matter. Missing ones usually don't.
- Tanuja

qa.q: What did Tanuja react with every time?
qa.a: Tanuja reacted with a heart every time, sometimes a folded-hands one.

qa.q: What was Tanuja worried about when sending only hearts?
qa.a: Tanuja was anxious that the hearts were too small and that Eshaan would think it was lazy support.

qa.q: Which of Tanuja's choices worked, and why?
qa.a: Sending quiet hearts worked, because Eshaan didn't want to talk but still felt seen, and later asking lightly cleared up the missing reactions.

qa.q: How did Eshaan see the hearts during that time?
qa.a: He saw them as a sign someone noticed, which comforted him without pressuring him to talk.

grounding: The account shows reaction buttons as lightweight support and a missing reaction not being over-read as rejection.

passage:
Choir supervisor's note, Wednesday
Gargi was quiet all through warm-ups today, which is unusual. At break she showed me the group chat: on Sunday she had posted a recording of her solo, and in three days it had one reaction, a thumbs-up from Joseph. "Everyone listened and nobody liked it," she said, voice tight. I told her reactions are small, quick things; lots of people read and move on, and a missing one isn't a verdict. She didn't look convinced. So I asked the group, casually, who had heard Gargi's recording. Eleven hands went up. Two said they had played it twice on the bus. Joseph said his thumbs-up meant "that high note, wow". Gargi laughed and covered her face. Afterwards I suggested to the group that if something moves us, a line of words is worth sending. I'll keep an eye on how Gargi is on Friday.

qa.q: How many reactions did Gargi's recording get in three days?
qa.a: It had one reaction, a thumbs-up from Joseph.

qa.q: What was Gargi feeling when she said 'nobody liked it'?
qa.a: Gargi felt hurt and discouraged, voice tight, reading the missing reactions as rejection; part of it may also have been nerves about the solo itself.

qa.q: What did the supervisor do that helped?
qa.a: The supervisor explained that reactions are lightweight, then checked with the group, which showed eleven people had listened, and encouraged sending words when something moves them.

qa.q: What did Joseph's thumbs-up mean to Joseph?
qa.a: To Joseph it meant 'that high note, wow', a quick sign of real admiration rather than a lukewarm one.

grounding: It shows reaction buttons as lightweight signals of support, and a teenager learning that a missing reaction does not mean rejection.
